<reason>Both sides were sharp, disciplined, and format-compliant, with clean A1:/A2: answers and genuinely pointed questions. A built a real route: the distinction between legible scope and an individual veto, plus the distributive claim that a veto empowers stars and estates while stranding day players and small-market dubs. But A's own concessions cost it. Once A said "itemization without veto is fine" and admitted that within faithful dubbing there is no use a fairly paid performer would refuse, the debate narrowed to precisely the ground B chose: who bears the default duty to ask, and whether protections A promises (deletion, no-training, reuse fees) can attach to a right nobody knew they granted. B's "prices come from the possibility of refusal" and "a right you cannot refuse is a tariff" gave a clean decision rule; B also defused A's strongest practical objection by locating consent at hiring, before localization spend, which drained most of the hostage/collapse scenario (A's estate/deceased-performer slice survived, but was minor and underdeveloped). B's reframe that timbre is the mechanism while permanence is the harm answered A's "fidelity is not forgery" better than A's rejoinder that "a veto doesn't delete a file" answered B, since B had already shown that enforcement of deletion presupposes an identified grant. A's best surviving hit — that collective bargaining, not individual opt-in, is the real source of leverage — was plausible and slightly under-answered by B, which keeps the margin competitive rather than dominant.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's exploitation of A's concession: after A conceded "itemization without veto is fine" and that broad contracts already wall uses by picture, term, and training, B pinned the case to a single question — whether the performer may say no — and argued that every protection A promised requires a discrete, identifiable right to attach to and a possible refusal to price it. That collapsed A's position toward PRO's substance while leaving A only the veto-as-hostage objection, which B had already answered by placing consent at the hiring session.</best_rebuttal>
